# 1. Research Environment and Setup

## 1.1 Required R Libraries
```{r}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)
library(stringdist)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(MatchIt)
library(cobalt)
library(broom)
```

The analysis was conducted in R using packages for data manipulation, visualization, statistical modeling, and causal inference. The `haven`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `stringr` packages support data import, cleaning, and organization, while `ggplot2` and `knitr` are used to generate figures and tables. The `sandwich` and `lmtest` packages support regression diagnostics and robust standard errors. Finally, `MatchIt` and `cobalt` are used to implement matching and evaluate covariate balance, while `broom` assists with organizing model outputs.

## 1.2 Output Directories and Reproducibility

```{r}
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("outputs/tables", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("outputs/figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("outputs/data", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("outputs/models", showWarnings = FALSE)

set.seed(4422)

getwd()
```

The project was configured to store generated tables, figures, processed datasets, and statistical models in separate directories to maintain an organized and reproducible workflow. A random seed of 4422 was established to support reproducibility in subsequent statistical analyses. The working directory was also verified to ensure that outputs are saved within the intended econometrics project folder.

# 2. Data Collection and Preparation

## 2.1 Importing the BAAD and NAG Datasets

```{r}
BAAD_raw <- read_sav(
  "/Users/katelynmccullough/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-FloridaPolytechnicUniversity/Florida Polytechnic University/Econometrics/ECO4422_Project/BAAD_Files/BAAD_Database.sav"
)

active_raw <- read.csv("~/Downloads/Monadic_Rebel_Group_active_support.csv", sep = ";")
passive_raw <- read.csv("~/Downloads/Monadic_Rebel_Group_defacto_support.csv", sep = ";")

# Check imported dimensions
dim(BAAD_raw)
dim(active_raw)
dim(passive_raw)

# Inspect variable names
names(BAAD_raw)
names(active_raw)
names(passive_raw)
```

Three datasets were imported for the analysis. The Big Allied and Dangerous (BAAD) dataset contains 395 terrorist organizations and 19 variables, including state sponsorship, organizational characteristics, and recorded fatalities from 1998 to 2005. Two supplementary Non-State Armed Groups (NAG) datasets were imported to examine active and de facto forms of state support. Each contains 6,910 observations, with 15 variables describing active support and 14 describing de facto support. The dimensions and variable names were inspected to confirm successful import and identify the variables required for subsequent data processing and merging.

## 2.2 Data Validation and Integrity Checks

```{r}
# Required BAAD variables

baad_required <- c(
  "mastertccode3606",
  "group",
  "statespond",
  "fatalities19982005",
  "OrgAge",
  "ordsize",
  "terrStrong",
  "degree",
  "ContainRelig",
  "ContainEthno"
)

missing_baad <- setdiff(
  baad_required,
  names(BAAD_raw)
)

if (length(missing_baad) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Missing BAAD variables: ",
    paste(missing_baad, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

# Required NAG variables

active_required <- c(
  "NagCode_1",
  "NagCode_2",
  "Nag_Name",
  "Year",
  "NumNAG_S"
)

passive_required <- c(
  "NagCode_1",
  "NagCode_2",
  "Nag_Name",
  "Year",
  "NumNAG_DS"
)

stopifnot(
  all(active_required %in% names(active_raw)),
  all(passive_required %in% names(passive_raw))
)

# Verify organization-level uniqueness
baad_duplicates <- BAAD_raw %>%
  count(mastertccode3606) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

print(baad_duplicates)

if (nrow(baad_duplicates) > 0) {
  stop("Duplicate BAAD organization IDs detected.")
}

# Sponsorship and fatality validation
stopifnot(
  all(
    na.omit(as.numeric(BAAD_raw$statespond)) %in%
      c(0, 1)
  ),
  all(
    na.omit(
      as.numeric(BAAD_raw$fatalities19982005)
    ) >= 0
  )
)

# Check missing values in primary variables

BAAD_raw %>%
  summarise(
    missing_sponsorship = sum(is.na(statespond)),
    missing_fatalities = sum(is.na(fatalities19982005)),
    missing_organization_ids = sum(is.na(mastertccode3606))
  )
```

Data integrity checks were conducted before merging and analyzing the datasets. All required variables were present in their respective datasets, and no duplicate organization identifiers were detected in BAAD, confirming that each organization has a unique recorded identifier. State sponsorship values were verified to follow the expected binary coding, and fatality counts were confirmed to be nonnegative. These checks establish that the imported data meet the basic structural and coding requirements for subsequent analysis, although they do not independently establish the accuracy of the original measurements.

## 2.3 Restricting the NAG Data to the Study Period

```{r}
# Restrict NAG observations to 1998–2005

active <- active_raw %>%
  filter(between(Year, 1998, 2005))

passive <- passive_raw %>%
  filter(between(Year, 1998, 2005))

dim(active)
dim(passive)
```

Both NAG datasets were restricted to observations recorded between 1998 and 2005 to align with the BAAD study period. Following this restriction, the active and de facto support datasets each contained 883 observations, retaining 15 and 14 variables, respectively. This ensures that subsequent measures of state support are constructed using records from the same eight-year period as the organizational fatality outcome.

## 2.4 Verifying Unique Organization-Year Records

```{r}
# Each organization-code combination should have
# at most one observation per year.

nag_keys <- c(
  "NagCode_1",
  "NagCode_2",
  "Year"
)

active_duplicates <- active %>%
  count(across(all_of(nag_keys))) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

passive_duplicates <- passive %>%
  count(across(all_of(nag_keys))) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

print(active_duplicates)
print(passive_duplicates)

if (
  nrow(active_duplicates) > 0 ||
  nrow(passive_duplicates) > 0
) {
  stop(
    "Duplicate NAG year keys detected. ",
    "Review the unit of observation before joining."
  )
}
```

The active and de facto support datasets were examined for duplicate records using the combination of `NagCode_1`, `NagCode_2`, and `Year` as a unique identifier. Neither dataset contained duplicate combinations of these variables, indicating that each organization-code combination appears at most once per year. This confirms that the selected keys are unique within each dataset and can be used to merge the two sources without introducing duplicate observations through repeated keys.

## 2.5 Merging Active and De Facto State Support Records

```{r}
# Preserve organization names from either source

support <- active %>%
  rename(Nag_Name_active = Nag_Name) %>%
  full_join(
    passive %>%
      rename(Nag_Name_passive = Nag_Name),
    by = nag_keys,
    suffix = c("_active", "_passive")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Nag_Name = coalesce(
      Nag_Name_active,
      Nag_Name_passive
    )
  )

# Verify complete overlap between the two datasets

active_only_records <- anti_join(
  active,
  passive,
  by = nag_keys
)

passive_only_records <- anti_join(
  passive,
  active,
  by = nag_keys
)

cat(
  "Active-only records:", nrow(active_only_records), "\n",
  "De facto-only records:", nrow(passive_only_records), "\n"
)

dim(support)
names(support)
```
The active and de facto state support datasets were merged using the organization identifiers `NagCode_1` and `NagCode_2` together with the observation year. A full join was used to preserve records appearing in either dataset, and organization names were consolidated into a common variable while retaining the original source-specific names. The resulting dataset contains 883 observations and 27 variables, combining information on both forms of state support for the 1998–2005 study period. The unchanged observation count is consistent with complete overlap between the two datasets, subject to verification of their joining keys.

## 2.6 Classifying Active and De Facto State Support

```{r}
# Keep missing support values distinct from zero

support <- support %>%
  mutate(
    active_recorded = case_when(
      is.na(NumNAG_S) ~ NA_integer_,
      NumNAG_S > 0 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L
    ),
    passive_recorded = case_when(
      is.na(NumNAG_DS) ~ NA_integer_,
      NumNAG_DS > 0 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L
    )
  )

support %>%
  count(
    active_recorded,
    passive_recorded,
    name = "observations"
  )

# Inspect observations with both types of support

support %>%
  filter(
    active_recorded == 1,
    passive_recorded == 1
  ) %>%
  select(
    Nag_Name,
    Year,
    NumNAG_S,
    NumNAG_DS,
    any_of(c(
      "Num_S_FinAid",
      "Num_DS_FinAid",
      "Num_S_WeaponLog",
      "Num_DS_WeaponLog"
    ))
  ) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  print(n = 10)
```

Binary indicators were constructed to identify whether each organization received active or de facto state support during a given year, while preserving missing observations separately from recorded zeros. Of the 883 organization-year records, 298 (33.7%) exhibited both types of support, 185 (21.0%) recorded active support only, and 194 (22.0%) recorded de facto support only. The remaining 206 observations (23.3%) recorded neither type. Additional inspection of organizations receiving both forms of support provided information on specific assistance categories, including financial aid and weapons logistics. These classifications establish the basis for examining patterns of state assistance over the study period.

## 2.7 Aggregating State Support to the Organization Level

```{r}
# Aggregate NAG observations across 1998–2005

support_summary <- support %>%
  group_by(
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    Nag_Name = first(
      Nag_Name[!is.na(Nag_Name)],
      default = NA_character_
    ),

    years_observed = n_distinct(Year),

    years_active_observed = sum(
      !is.na(active_recorded)
    ),

    years_passive_observed = sum(
      !is.na(passive_recorded)
    ),

    years_active = sum(
      active_recorded == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    years_passive = sum(
      passive_recorded == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),

    any_active = as.integer(
      years_active > 0
    ),

    any_passive = as.integer(
      years_passive > 0
    ),

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    support_type = case_when(
      any_active == 1 & any_passive == 1 ~ "Both",
      any_active == 1 ~ "Active only",
      any_passive == 1 ~ "Passive only",
      years_active_observed > 0 &
        years_passive_observed > 0 ~ "Neither recorded",
      TRUE ~ "Incomplete support information"
    )
  )

# Support categories
support_summary %>%
  count(support_type)

# Save NAG summary
write.csv(
  support_summary,
  "outputs/data/nag_support_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Annual state support observations were aggregated into organization-level records covering the 1998–2005 study period. The aggregation measured the number of observed years, the number of years with active or de facto support, and whether each support type occurred at least once. The initial classification identified 160 organization-code combinations, including 62 (38.75%) receiving both forms of support, 30 (18.75%) receiving active support only, 32 (20.00%) receiving de facto support only, and 36 (22.50%) with neither form recorded. These organization-level measures were exported for subsequent matching with the BAAD dataset. The final category counts should be confirmed after applying the revised missing-data classification.

## 2.8 Standardizing Organization Names for Dataset Matching

```{r}
# Standardize names for exact string matching

clean_group_name <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    str_to_lower() %>%
    str_remove_all("\\([^)]*\\)") %>%
    str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9]", "") %>%
    str_trim()
}

support_summary <- support_summary %>%
  mutate(
    match_name = clean_group_name(Nag_Name)
  )

BAAD <- BAAD_raw %>%
  mutate(
    match_name = clean_group_name(group)
  )

# Check for ambiguous standardized NAG names

ambiguous_names <- support_summary %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(match_name),
    match_name != ""
  ) %>%
  count(match_name) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

print(ambiguous_names)

# Inspect ambiguous standardized organization names

ambiguous_details <- support_summary %>%
  semi_join(
    ambiguous_names,
    by = "match_name"
  ) %>%
  select(
    match_name,
    Nag_Name,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2
  ) %>%
  arrange(match_name, NagCode_1, NagCode_2)

print(ambiguous_details, n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

Organization names were standardized across the BAAD and NAG datasets to facilitate record linkage despite differences in capitalization, punctuation, and abbreviated names. The standardization procedure converted names to lowercase and removed parenthetical text and nonalphanumeric characters. A diagnostic check identified six standardized names associated with multiple NAG organization-code combinations, indicating potential ambiguity in name-based matching. These cases require additional verification to avoid incorrectly linking distinct organizations or organizational factions during the subsequent merge.

## 2.9 Identifying State-Sponsored Organizations in BAAD

```{r}
BAAD_sponsored <- BAAD %>%
  filter(statespond == 1)

# Count sponsored organizations
nrow(BAAD_sponsored)

# Count nonsponsored organizations
BAAD %>%
  count(statespond)
```

The BAAD dataset was divided according to the binary state sponsorship indicator to establish the treatment and comparison groups for subsequent analysis. Of the 395 terrorist organizations, 32 (8.10%) were classified as state-sponsored, while 363 (91.90%) were classified as nonsponsored. The sponsored organizations were isolated for subsequent linkage with the NAG support records. The relatively small sponsored group highlights the imbalance in treatment-group sizes and motivates the use of matching methods to construct more comparable treatment and control samples.

## 2.10 Identifying Exact Organization-Name Matches

```{r}
# Exact normalized-name matches

matched_sponsored <- BAAD_sponsored %>%
  inner_join(
    support_summary,
    by = "match_name",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )

# Inspect matched organizations
matched_sponsored %>%
  select(
    mastertccode3606,
    group,
    Nag_Name,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2,
    fatalities19982005,
    support_type,
    years_active,
    years_passive
  ) %>%
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

# Count unique BAAD organizations matched
n_distinct(matched_sponsored$mastertccode3606)
```

An initial record-linkage procedure was conducted by joining state-sponsored BAAD organizations to NAG records using standardized organization names. This procedure identified 11 unique matches among the 32 sponsored BAAD organizations, representing 34.38% of the sponsored sample. The matched records include organizational fatality counts, active and de facto support classifications, and the number of years each support type was observed. The remaining 21 sponsored organizations were not matched through the initial name-standardization procedure and require further investigation of alternative names, abbreviations, or organizational identities.

## 2.11 Identifying Unmatched State-Sponsored Organizations

```{r}
unmatched_sponsored <- BAAD_sponsored %>%
  anti_join(
    support_summary %>%
      filter(
        !is.na(match_name),
        match_name != ""
      ) %>%
      distinct(match_name),
    by = "match_name"
  ) %>%
  select(
    mastertccode3606,
    group,
    cowmastercountry,
    fatalities19982005
  )

print(
  unmatched_sponsored,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

nrow(unmatched_sponsored)
```

Following the initial standardized-name matching procedure, an anti-join was used to identify state-sponsored BAAD organizations without corresponding NAG records. This identified 21 unmatched organizations, representing 65.62% of the 32 sponsored organizations in BAAD. The unmatched records were retained with their organizational identifiers, names, countries, and fatality counts to support further examination. Several organizations may be represented under alternative names or abbreviations in the NAG data, making additional name verification necessary before constructing the final merged dataset.

## 2.12 Constructing and Validating a Manual Organization Crosswalk

```{r}
crosswalk <- tibble(
  group = c(
    "National Liberation Army (Colombia)",
    "Lord's Resistance Army (LRA)",
    "Mahdi Army",
    "Taliban",
    "Hamas",
    "al-Fatah"
  ),
  Nag_Name = c(
    "The National Liberation Army (ELN)",
    "The Lord's Resistance Army",
    "Al-Mahdi Army",
    "Taleban",
    "Islamic Resistance Movement",
    "Fatah"
  )
)

crosswalk_check <- crosswalk %>%
  left_join(
    support_summary,
    by = "Nag_Name",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  select(
    group,
    Nag_Name,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2,
    support_type,
    years_active,
    years_passive
  )

print(crosswalk_check, n = Inf)

# Which proposed names were not found?
crosswalk_check %>%
  filter(is.na(NagCode_1))
```

A manual organization-name crosswalk was constructed to identify potential matches that were not captured by the initial standardized-name procedure. Six BAAD organizations were associated with alternative names recorded in the NAG dataset, including differences in spelling, abbreviations, and organizational naming conventions. All six proposed NAG names were located successfully, and the resulting records provided corresponding organization codes and state support classifications. These candidate links expand the potential coverage of the BAAD–NAG merge, although organizational identity must be verified before the mappings are incorporated into the final analytical dataset.

## 2.13 Evaluating Additional Candidate Organization Matches

```{r}
candidate_matches <- tibble::tribble(
  ~group, ~NagCode_1, ~match_status,

  "National Liberation Army (Colombia)",
  408, "Alias",

  "Lord's Resistance Army (LRA)",
  300, "Alias",

  "Mahdi Army",
  73, "Alias",

  "Taliban",
  143, "Alias",

  "Hamas",
  50, "Alias",

  "al-Fatah",
  48, "Alias",

  "Salafist Group for Call and Combat (GSPC)",
  351, "Historical name - coding review",

  "Eritrean Islamic Jihad Movement (EIJM)",
  307, "Possible subgroup",

  "Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF)",
  119, "Possible faction"
)

candidate_check <- candidate_matches %>%
  left_join(
    support_summary,
    by = "NagCode_1",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  select(
    group,
    Nag_Name,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2,
    match_status,
    years_observed,
    years_active,
    years_passive
  )

print(candidate_check, n = Inf, width = Inf)

# Investigate selected organization codes

support_summary %>%
  filter(NagCode_1 %in% c(351, 482)) %>%
  select(
    Nag_Name,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2,
    years_observed,
    years_active,
    years_passive,
    support_type
  ) %>%
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

The manual matching procedure was expanded to examine nine candidate links between BAAD and NAG organizations. Six candidates were retained as previously identified aliases, while three additional cases were flagged for further investigation because of possible historical renaming, subgroup relationships, or organizational faction differences. Examination of the Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb records identified two distinct NAG organization codes with different recorded support classifications, illustrating the risk of assigning support information based on similar names alone. Consequently, the three uncertain candidates were retained for review but excluded from the verified matching procedure to reduce the risk of misclassification.

## 2.14 Consolidating and Validating BAAD–NAG Organization Matches

```{r}
# Exact matches with unique organization identifiers

exact_matches <- matched_sponsored %>%
  select(
    mastertccode3606,
    group,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2
  ) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  mutate(match_method = "Exact name")

# Candidate aliases that were previously reviewed

alias_matches <- candidate_matches %>%
  filter(match_status == "Alias") %>%
  select(
    group,
    NagCode_1
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    BAAD %>%
      select(mastertccode3606, group),
    by = "group"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    support_summary %>%
      select(
        NagCode_1,
        NagCode_2,
        Nag_Name
      ),
    by = "NagCode_1",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  mutate(match_method = "Manual alias")

# Inspect all candidate alias combinations

print(
  alias_matches,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

# Check for missing keys
unresolved_aliases <- alias_matches %>%
  filter(
    is.na(mastertccode3606) |
    is.na(NagCode_1) |
    is.na(NagCode_2)
  )

print(unresolved_aliases)

# Combine exact and alias matches

verified_matches <- bind_rows(
  exact_matches,
  alias_matches %>%
    select(
      mastertccode3606,
      group,
      NagCode_1,
      NagCode_2,
      match_method
    )
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(mastertccode3606),
    !is.na(NagCode_1),
    !is.na(NagCode_2)
  ) %>%
  distinct()

# A BAAD organization must not map to
# multiple distinct NAG code combinations.

ambiguous_matches <- verified_matches %>%
  distinct(
    mastertccode3606,
    NagCode_1,
    NagCode_2
  ) %>%
  count(mastertccode3606) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

print(ambiguous_matches)

if (nrow(ambiguous_matches) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Ambiguous BAAD-to-NAG matches detected. ",
    "Review the crosswalk before continuing."
  )
}

# One verified record per BAAD organization

verified_matches <- verified_matches %>%
  arrange(
    mastertccode3606,
    desc(match_method == "Exact name")
  ) %>%
  distinct(mastertccode3606, .keep_all = TRUE)

nrow(verified_matches)

```

The standardized-name matches and manually identified aliases were consolidated into a single BAAD–NAG organization crosswalk. The procedure combined 11 initial name matches with six additional alias matches, producing 17 unique linked organizations, or 53.13% of the 32 state-sponsored organizations in BAAD. Validation checks found no missing organization identifiers or cases in which a BAAD organization was assigned multiple distinct NAG codes. The resulting crosswalk provides the basis for integrating additional state support information into BAAD, while the 15 remaining unmatched organizations are retained separately to avoid assigning unsupported organizational identities.

## 2.15 Assessing Final BAAD–NAG Matching Coverage

```{r}
# Organizations successfully linked to NAG

matched_groups <- verified_matches %>%
  pull(mastertccode3606)

# Sponsored organizations still unmatched

still_unmatched <- BAAD_sponsored %>%
  filter(
    !mastertccode3606 %in% matched_groups
  ) %>%
  select(
    mastertccode3606,
    group,
    cowmastercountry,
    fatalities19982005
  )

print(
  still_unmatched,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

# Match summary

match_summary <- tibble(
  total_sponsored = nrow(BAAD_sponsored),

  verified_matches = n_distinct(
    verified_matches$mastertccode3606
  ),

  still_unmatched = nrow(still_unmatched),

  match_rate = 100 *
    verified_matches /
    total_sponsored
)
```

Following the consolidation of standardized-name and manual alias matches, 15 of the 32 state-sponsored BAAD organizations remained unmatched to the NAG dataset. The combined matching procedure therefore linked 17 organizations, representing 53.13% of the sponsored sample. The remaining 15 organizations were retained for documentation rather than assigned uncertain NAG identities. This distinction is important because incomplete record linkage limits the coverage of supplementary active and de facto support classifications, although the unmatched organizations remain available for the primary BAAD-based analysis of state sponsorship and fatalities.

## 2.16 Exporting the Organization Matching Results

```{r}
match_summary <- tibble(
  total_sponsored = nrow(BAAD_sponsored),
  verified_matches = nrow(verified_matches),
  still_unmatched = nrow(still_unmatched)
) %>%
  mutate(
    match_rate = 100 *
      verified_matches / total_sponsored
  )

print(match_summary)

write.csv(
  match_summary,
  "outputs/tables/nag_match_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  still_unmatched,
  "outputs/tables/nag_unmatched_groups.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  verified_matches,
  "outputs/data/verified_nag_crosswalk.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The final organization-matching results were summarized and exported for documentation and reproducibility. Of the 32 state-sponsored organizations in BAAD, 17 (53.13%) were linked to NAG records, while 15 (46.88%) remained unmatched. Three CSV files were generated to preserve the matching summary, the list of unmatched organizations, and the accepted organization crosswalk. These outputs provide a record of the linkage procedure and allow the supplementary state support classifications to be traced to their corresponding organizational identifiers in subsequent analyses.

## 2.17 Constructing the Final BAAD–NAG Analytical Dataset

```{r}
matched_support <- verified_matches %>%
  left_join(
    support_summary %>%
      select(
        NagCode_1,
        NagCode_2,
        support_type,
        years_observed,
        years_active_observed,
        years_passive_observed,
        years_active,
        years_passive,
        any_active,
        any_passive
      ),
    by = c("NagCode_1", "NagCode_2"),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

BAAD_combined <- BAAD %>%
  left_join(
    matched_support %>%
      select(-group),
    by = "mastertccode3606",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

# Confirm merge preserved every BAAD observation

stopifnot(
  nrow(BAAD_combined) == nrow(BAAD)
)

dim(BAAD_combined)

BAAD_combined %>%
  count(statespond, support_type)

# Save merged data

saveRDS(
  BAAD_combined,
  "outputs/data/BAAD_combined.rds"
)

write.csv(
  BAAD_combined,
  "outputs/data/BAAD_combined.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The accepted BAAD–NAG organization crosswalk was used to integrate supplementary state support information into the full BAAD dataset. The resulting dataset retained all 395 organizations and contained 31 variables, including the original sponsorship and fatality measures alongside the linked NAG support indicators. Among the 32 state-sponsored organizations, 17 were linked to NAG records: 13 were classified as receiving both active and de facto support, two as receiving active support only, and two as receiving de facto support only. The remaining 15 sponsored organizations and all 363 nonsponsored organizations retained missing NAG classifications because no crosswalk links were assigned. The completed dataset was exported in RDS and CSV formats for subsequent statistical analysis.

# 3. Variable Construction and Descriptive Analysis

## 3.1 Constructing Outcome, Treatment, and Control Variables

```{r}
analysis_data <- BAAD_combined %>%
  mutate(
    fatalities = as.numeric(fatalities19982005),

    sponsored = as.numeric(statespond),

    positive_fatalities = case_when(
      is.na(fatalities) ~ NA_integer_,
      fatalities > 0 ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 0L
    ),

    log_fatalities = log1p(fatalities),

    OrgAge = as.numeric(OrgAge),
    ordsize = as.numeric(ordsize),
    terrStrong = as.numeric(terrStrong),
    degree = as.numeric(degree),

    containrelig = as.numeric(ContainRelig),
    containethno = as.numeric(ContainEthno),

    sponsorship_group = factor(
      sponsored,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c(
        "Not sponsored",
        "Sponsored"
      )
    )
  )

# Preserve categorical size variable for regression

analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    size_category = factor(ordsize),

    age_group = case_when(
      is.na(OrgAge) ~ NA_character_,
      OrgAge < 10 ~ "Under 10 years",
      OrgAge < 20 ~ "10–19 years",
      OrgAge < 30 ~ "20–29 years",
      TRUE ~ "30+ years"
    ),

    age_group = factor(
      age_group,
      levels = c(
        "Under 10 years",
        "10–19 years",
        "20–29 years",
        "30+ years"
      )
    )
  )

# Verify numeric variables

summary(
  analysis_data %>%
    select(
      fatalities,
      sponsored,
      OrgAge,
      ordsize,
      terrStrong,
      degree,
      containrelig,
      containethno
    )
)
```

The merged dataset was transformed to construct the variables required for descriptive and econometric analysis. Recorded fatalities were retained on their original scale and converted into a binary indicator of whether an organization caused at least one fatality, as well as a log-transformed measure to accommodate the strongly right-skewed outcome distribution. State sponsorship was represented as a binary treatment indicator, while organizational age, size, territorial strength, network degree, and ideological characteristics were prepared as potential control variables. Additional categorical variables were constructed for organizational size, age, and sponsorship status. Initial descriptive statistics indicated a mean of 31.36 fatalities and a median of zero, highlighting substantial variation in organizational lethality.

## 3.2 Missing Data Assessment

```{r}
# Missing observations by variable

variables_to_check <- c(
  "fatalities",
  "sponsored",
  "OrgAge",
  "ordsize",
  "terrStrong",
  "degree",
  "containrelig",
  "containethno"
)

missing_summary <- analysis_data %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      all_of(variables_to_check),
      list(
        missing = ~ sum(is.na(.x)),
        pct_missing = ~ 100 * mean(is.na(.x))
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c("variable", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "^(.*?)_(pct_missing|missing)$"
  )

print(missing_summary, n = Inf)

write.csv(
  missing_summary,
  "outputs/tables/missing_data_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Missingness by sponsorship

missing_by_sponsorship <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(sponsorship_group) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),

    missing_fatalities = sum(is.na(fatalities)),
    missing_age = sum(is.na(OrgAge)),
    missing_size = sum(is.na(ordsize)),
    missing_territory = sum(is.na(terrStrong)),
    missing_degree = sum(is.na(degree)),

    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(missing_by_sponsorship)
```

Missing-data diagnostics were conducted for the primary outcome, treatment indicator, and six organizational control variables. No missing observations were identified among the 395 organizations for any of the eight variables examined. Additional checks by sponsorship status confirmed that the selected variables were complete for both the 32 sponsored and 363 nonsponsored organizations. Consequently, the primary regression and matching analyses can use the full BAAD sample without excluding observations due to missing values in these variables. This completeness does not extend to the supplementary NAG support classifications, which are available only for organizations successfully linked across datasets.

```{r}
# Display as a regular R tibble
```

Overall descriptive statistics were calculated for the 395 organizations in the BAAD dataset. Of these organizations, 32 were classified as state-sponsored and 363 as nonsponsored. The mean number of recorded fatalities was 31.36, while the median was zero, indicating a highly right-skewed distribution in which many organizations recorded no fatalities. Fatality counts ranged from zero to 3,505, with a standard deviation of 202.04, demonstrating substantial variation in organizational lethality. No missing observations were identified for the fatality outcome.

## 3.5 Fatality Incidence by State Sponsorship

```{r}
# Fatality incidence by state sponsorship

fatality_incidence <- analysis_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(sponsored),
    !is.na(fatalities)
  ) %>%
  group_by(sponsorship_group) %>%
  summarise(

    ),

    groups_without_fatalities = sum(

    ),

    pct_without_fatalities = 100 *

    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Verify that group totals are consistent

stopifnot(

    fatality_incidence$total_groups ==
      fatality_incidence$groups_with_fatalities +
      fatality_incidence$groups_without_fatalities
  )
)

# Display as a regular R tibble

print(
  fatality_incidence %>%
    mutate(
      across(
        starts_with("pct_"),
        ~ round(.x, 2)
      )
    ),
  width = Inf
)

# Export full-precision results

write.csv(
  fatality_incidence,
  "outputs/tables/fatality_incidence.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Fatality incidence was examined by calculating the proportion of organizations recording at least one fatality during the 1998–2005 study period. Among state-sponsored organizations, 24 of 32 (75.00%) recorded fatalities, compared with 131 of 363 (36.09%) nonsponsored organizations. This represents a difference of approximately 38.91 percentage points. Conversely, 25.00% of sponsored organizations and 63.91% of nonsponsored organizations recorded zero fatalities. These findings indicate a substantial positive descriptive association between state sponsorship and the likelihood of recording fatalities, although further analysis is necessary to account for differences in organizational characteristics.

Organizational characteristics were compared across sponsored and nonsponsored groups to identify differences potentially associated with state sponsorship and lethality. Sponsored organizations were substantially older on average, with a mean age of 23.84 years compared with 10.16 years among nonsponsored organizations. They also exhibited higher average size categories (1.50 versus 0.43), greater territorial strength (43.75% versus 7.99%), and more network connections (3.16 versus 1.23). # 5. Regression Analysis and Model Specification

## 5.1 Regression Sample Construction

```{r}
# Main baseline sample

baseline_data <- analysis_data %>%
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      fatalities,
      sponsored
    )
  )

# Common complete-case sample for adjusted models

regression_data <- analysis_data %>%
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      fatalities,
      sponsored,
      OrgAge,
      ordsize,
      terrStrong,
      degree,
      containrelig,
      containethno
    )
  )

sample_counts <- tibble(
  sample = c(
    "Full BAAD",
    "Baseline regression",
    "Adjusted regression"
  ),

  observations = c(
    nrow(analysis_data),
    nrow(baseline_data),
    nrow(regression_data)
  ),

  sponsored = c(
    sum(analysis_data$sponsored == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(baseline_data$sponsored == 1),
    sum(regression_data$sponsored == 1)
  )
)

print(sample_counts)

write.csv(
  sample_counts,
  "outputs/tables/regression_sample_counts.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Two regression samples were constructed to ensure consistent treatment of missing observations across the econometric specifications. The baseline sample required complete information on recorded fatalities and state sponsorship, while the adjusted sample additionally required complete observations for organizational age, size, territorial strength, network degree, and ideological indicators. Both samples retained all 395 BAAD organizations, including 32 sponsored and 363 nonsponsored groups. Consequently, differences in coefficient estimates across the baseline and adjusted regressions cannot be attributed to changes in sample composition caused by missing data. The resulting samples provide a consistent basis for comparing unadjusted and covariate-adjusted associations between state sponsorship and organizational lethality.

## 5.2 Baseline OLS Regression: State Sponsorship and Fatalities

```{r}
model1 <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~ sponsored,
  data = baseline_data
)

summary(model1)

coeftest(
  model1,
  vcov. = vcovHC(
    model1,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)
```

An initial ordinary least squares regression was estimated to examine the unadjusted association between state sponsorship and organizational lethality, measured as the natural logarithm of one plus recorded fatalities. The estimated sponsorship coefficient was positive (1.6451) and statistically significant using HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (SE = 0.3873, p < 0.001). This indicates that sponsored organizations exhibited significantly higher average log-transformed fatalities than nonsponsored organizations before controlling for other characteristics. However, the model explained only 7.53% of the variation in the outcome, and the coefficient cannot be interpreted as causal because potentially important organizational differences remain unaccounted for. Subsequent models introduce additional covariates to assess the robustness of this association.

## 5.3 Adjusted OLS Regression: Organizational Characteristics

```{r}
# Model 2: OLS with organizational controls

model2 <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    factor(ordsize) +
    terrStrong +
    degree,
  data = regression_data
)

# Conventional OLS results

summary(model2)

# HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust results

model2_robust <- lmtest::coeftest(
  model2,
  vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(
    model2,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)

print(model2_robust)

```

A second OLS regression was estimated to examine the relationship between state sponsorship and organizational lethality after controlling for organizational age, size, territorial strength, and network degree. The sponsorship coefficient decreased from 1.6451 in the unadjusted model to 0.2885 and was no longer statistically significant (HC3 robust SE = 0.3578, p = 0.420). Organizational size and network degree remained positively and significantly associated with fatalities, while territorial strength and organizational age were not significant at the 5% level. The model explained approximately 40.3% of the variation in log-transformed fatalities. These findings suggest that organizational characteristics account for a substantial portion of the initially observed sponsorship association, although the adjusted relationship cannot be interpreted as causal.

## 5.4 OLS Regression with Organizational Age and Ideological Controls

```{r}
model3 <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(model3)

coeftest(
  model3,
  vcov. = vcovHC(
    model3,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)
```

A third OLS regression was estimated to examine the relationship between state sponsorship and organizational lethality while controlling for organizational age and ideological characteristics. The sponsorship coefficient remained positive and statistically significant (β = 0.9029, HC3 robust SE = 0.4130, p = 0.029). Organizational age and religious ideology were also positively and significantly associated with log-transformed fatalities, while ethnonationalist ideology was not statistically significant. The model explained approximately 22.2% of the variation in fatalities. Compared with the previous specification, these findings suggest that the estimated sponsorship association is sensitive to the inclusion of organizational capacity variables, emphasizing the importance of model specification when interpreting the results.

## 5.5 Fully Adjusted OLS Regression

```{r}
model4 <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno +
    factor(ordsize) +
    terrStrong +
    degree,
  data = regression_data
)

summary(model4)

coeftest(
  model4,
  vcov. = vcovHC(
    model4,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)
```

The final OLS specification incorporated organizational age, ideological characteristics, size, territorial strength, and network degree to examine the association between state sponsorship and organizational lethality after adjustment for all selected covariates. The sponsorship coefficient decreased to 0.0890 and was not statistically significant using HC3 robust standard errors (SE = 0.3605, p = 0.805). In contrast, religious ideology, organizational size, territorial strength, and network degree exhibited positive and statistically significant associations with log-transformed fatalities. The model explained approximately 45.0% of the variation in the outcome. These results indicate that the positive sponsorship association observed in the baseline model is substantially attenuated after accounting for organizational characteristics, although the possibility that some controls are influenced by sponsorship limits causal interpretation.

## 5.6 Consolidated OLS Regression Results and Robust Confidence Intervals

```{r}
# Create a consistent HC3 regression results table

robust_results <- function(fitted_model, model_name) {

  # Robust variance-covariance matrix
  vcov_matrix <- sandwich::vcovHC(
    fitted_model,
    type = "HC3"
  )

  # Extract coefficients
  estimates <- stats::coef(fitted_model)

  # Extract robust standard errors
  standard_errors <- sqrt(diag(vcov_matrix))

  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals
  critical_value <- qt(
    0.975,
    df = df.residual(fitted_model)
  )

  # Sample size
  sample_size <- nobs(fitted_model)

  # Create results table
  results <- tibble(
    model = model_name,

    term = names(estimates),

    estimate = as.numeric(estimates),

    std_error = as.numeric(
      standard_errors[names(estimates)]
    ),

    ci_lower = estimate -
      critical_value * std_error,

    ci_upper = estimate +
      critical_value * std_error,

    n = sample_size
  )

  return(results)
}

# Combine all four regression models

regression_results <- bind_rows(
  robust_results(model1, "Unadjusted"),
  robust_results(model2, "Original controls"),
  robust_results(model3, "Ideology adjusted"),
  robust_results(model4, "Full controls")
)

# Display results
print(regression_results, n = Inf)

# Export results
write.csv(
  regression_results,
  "outputs/tables/regression_results.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Save models
saveRDS(
  list(
    model1 = model1,
    model2 = model2,
    model3 = model3,
    model4 = model4
  ),
  "outputs/models/ols_models.rds"
)
```

The results from all four OLS specifications were consolidated into a single table using HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. All models retained the same sample of 395 organizations, allowing coefficient differences to be compared without changes in sample composition. State sponsorship was positively and significantly associated with log-transformed fatalities in the unadjusted model and the specification controlling for organizational age and ideology. However, the sponsorship coefficient became smaller and statistically insignificant when organizational size, territorial strength, and network degree were included. In the fully adjusted model, the estimated coefficient was 0.0890, with a 95% confidence interval of approximately −0.620 to 0.798. These results demonstrate that the estimated sponsorship association is sensitive to model specification and suggest that organizational characteristics play an important role in explaining observed differences in lethality. The estimates remain associational rather than causal.

# 6. Matching Analysis

## 6.1 Matching Sample Construction

```{r}
# Matching uses the complete-case analytical sample

matching_data <- analysis_data %>%
  filter(
    complete.cases(
      fatalities,
      sponsored,
      OrgAge,
      containrelig,
      containethno
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    match_id = row_number()
  )

# Check sponsorship composition

matching_data %>%
  count(sponsored)

# Record sample retention

matching_sample_summary <- tibble(
  full_sample = nrow(analysis_data),

  matching_sample = nrow(matching_data),

  sponsored_available = sum(
    matching_data$sponsored == 1
  ),

  controls_available = sum(
    matching_data$sponsored == 0
  ),

  excluded_observations =
    nrow(analysis_data) - nrow(matching_data)
)

print(matching_sample_summary)

write.csv(
  matching_sample_summary,
  "outputs/tables/matching_sample_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A matching sample was constructed to compare state-sponsored organizations with nonsponsored organizations sharing similar observable characteristics. The sample required complete information on recorded fatalities, sponsorship status, organizational age, religious ideology, and ethnonationalist ideology. All 395 BAAD organizations met these requirements, including 32 sponsored and 363 nonsponsored organizations, resulting in no exclusions due to missing data. Retaining the full sample provides a consistent starting point for the matching analysis, although the number of organizations ultimately matched will depend on the availability of comparable controls. The matching approach is intended to reduce observable differences between sponsorship groups but cannot account for unmeasured confounding.

## 6.2 Propensity Score Matching and Matched Sample Construction

```{r}
set.seed(4422)

# Nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching
# ATT-oriented, 1:1, without replacement

match_model <- matchit(
  sponsored ~
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno,

  data = matching_data,

  method = "nearest",
  distance = "glm",

  estimand = "ATT",

  ratio = 1,
  replace = FALSE,

  caliper = 0.2,
  std.caliper = TRUE
)

# Matching summary

summary(
  match_model,
  standardize = TRUE
)

# Extract matched data

matched_data <- match.data(
  match_model,
  data = matching_data
)

# Ensure the match procedure retained observations

if (nrow(matched_data) == 0) {
  stop(
    "No observations retained after matching. ",
    "Review propensity-score overlap and caliper."
  )
}

matched_data %>%
  count(sponsored)

# Save matched observations

write.csv(
  matched_data,
  "outputs/data/matched_data.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

saveRDS(
  match_model,
  "outputs/models/propensity_match_model.rds"
)
```

Propensity score matching was conducted using 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching without replacement and a standardized caliper of 0.2. Propensity scores were estimated using organizational age, religious ideology, and ethnonationalist ideology. The procedure successfully matched 30 of the 32 sponsored organizations with 30 nonsponsored organizations, producing a matched sample of 60 observations. Matching substantially improved covariate balance, particularly for organizational age and religious ideology, with post-matching standardized mean differences below 0.1. However, ethnonationalist ideology retained a standardized mean difference of 0.267, indicating some remaining imbalance. Two sponsored organizations could not be matched within the specified caliper. Consequently, the matched sample provides a more comparable basis for examining differences in organizational lethality, although residual imbalance, unmatched organizations, and unobserved confounding limit causal interpretation.

## 6.3 Matching Retention by Sponsorship Status

```{r}
# Match retention by treatment group

matching_counts <- matching_data %>%
  group_by(sponsored) %>%
  summarise(
    available = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    matched_data %>%
      group_by(sponsored) %>%
      summarise(
        matched = n(),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = "sponsored"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    matched = replace_na(matched, 0L),

    unmatched = available - matched,

    pct_retained = 100 *
      matched / available
  )

# Display matching retention

print(matching_counts, width = Inf)

# Export matching retention results

write.csv(
  matching_counts,
  "outputs/tables/matching_counts.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

```

The matching procedure retained 30 of the 32 state-sponsored organizations, corresponding to a treatment-group retention rate of 93.75%. These organizations were matched with 30 nonsponsored organizations selected from the 363 available controls, resulting in a control-group retention rate of 8.26%. The relatively low control retention rate reflects the 1:1 matching design, which selects a limited number of comparison organizations rather than retaining the entire nonsponsored sample. Although most sponsored organizations were successfully matched, two remained unmatched within the specified caliper. Consequently, subsequent matched comparisons are based on the 30 retained sponsored organizations and their corresponding controls, limiting the generalizability of the results to all sponsored organizations in the original sample.

## 6.4 Covariate Balance Assessment After Matching

```{r}
# Covariate balance before and after matching

balance_results <- bal.tab(
  match_model,
  un = TRUE,
  thresholds = c(m = 0.1)
)

print(balance_results)

# Export the balance table

balance_table <- balance_results$Balance %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(
    var = "variable"
  )

write.csv(
  balance_table,
  "outputs/tables/matching_balance.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Covariate balance was evaluated before and after propensity score matching using standardized mean differences and a threshold of 0.1. Matching substantially reduced differences between sponsored and nonsponsored organizations in estimated propensity scores, organizational age, and religious ideology, with all three measures falling below the specified threshold. However, ethnonationalist ideology remained imbalanced, with a post-matching standardized mean difference of approximately 0.267. Overall, the matching procedure improved comparability between the treatment and control groups but did not achieve complete balance across all observed characteristics. This remaining imbalance should be considered when interpreting subsequent estimates of the relationship between state sponsorship and organizational lethality.

Figure 6 illustrates covariate balance before and after propensity score matching using absolute standardized mean differences. Matching substantially reduced differences between sponsored and nonsponsored organizations in estimated propensity scores, organizational age, and religious ideology, bringing these measures below the 0.1 balance threshold. However, ethnonationalist ideology remained above the threshold, with a post-matching standardized mean difference of approximately 0.267. Although the matching procedure improved overall comparability between the groups, the remaining imbalance indicates that the matched sample does not fully satisfy the selected balance criterion. This limitation should be considered when interpreting subsequent estimates of the relationship between state sponsorship and organizational lethality.

These patterns suggest that the matching procedure selected control organizations with observable characteristics more similar to those of the sponsored group. Nevertheless, overlap in propensity scores does not establish complete covariate balance, as residual differences in ethnonationalist ideology remain. The matched sample therefore improves comparability but does not eliminate potential confounding or establish a causal relationship between sponsorship and organizational lethality.

## 6.7 Validation of One-to-One Matched Pairs

```{r}
# Inspect matched-set structure

pair_structure <- matched_data %>%
  group_by(subclass) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    treated = sum(sponsored == 1),
    controls = sum(sponsored == 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(pair_structure)

# Require complete one-to-one matched sets

stopifnot(
  all(pair_structure$n == 2),
  all(pair_structure$treated == 1),
  all(pair_structure$controls == 1)
)
```

The matched sample was examined to verify the structure of the treatment-control pairs before estimating fatality differences. All 30 matched subclasses contained exactly two organizations, consisting of one state-sponsored organization and one nonsponsored control. This confirmed that the matching procedure produced 30 complete one-to-one pairs, totaling 60 observations. Validating the matched-pair structure ensures that subsequent comparisons can be calculated consistently within each pair, reducing the influence of observed differences in the characteristics used for matching. However, successful pair construction does not guarantee complete covariate balance or eliminate unobserved confounding.

## 6.8 Construction of Matched-Pair Fatality Differences

```{r}
# One observation per matched pair

matched_pairs <- matched_data %>%
  group_by(subclass) %>%
  summarise(
    treated_id = match_id[sponsored == 1],
    control_id = match_id[sponsored == 0],

    treated_fatalities =
      fatalities[sponsored == 1],

    control_fatalities =
      fatalities[sponsored == 0],

    treated_log =
      log_fatalities[sponsored == 1],

    control_log =
      log_fatalities[sponsored == 0],

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    fatality_difference =
      treated_fatalities -
      control_fatalities,

    log_difference =
      treated_log -
      control_log
  )

print(
  matched_pairs,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

write.csv(
  matched_pairs,
  "outputs/data/matched_pairs.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A matched-pair dataset was constructed to compare fatalities between each state-sponsored organization and its corresponding nonsponsored control. For all 30 matched pairs, differences were calculated using both raw fatality counts and log-transformed fatalities, with positive values indicating higher fatalities among sponsored organizations. The observed raw differences ranged from −356 to 345 fatalities, demonstrating substantial variation across matched pairs. Some sponsored organizations recorded considerably more fatalities than their controls, while others recorded fewer. These within-pair differences provide the basis for estimating the average matched association between state sponsorship and organizational lethality. However, variation across pairs and the remaining covariate imbalance require cautious interpretation of subsequent estimates.

The matched-pair dataset was validated to confirm its structure and suitability for subsequent analysis. The dataset contained 30 unique treatment-control pairs, with one sponsored and one nonsponsored organization per pair. Each pair included recorded fatalities and log-transformed fatalities for both organizations, along with their corresponding within-pair differences. Structural checks confirmed that the matched observations were uniquely identified and that the calculated differences contained no missing or nonfinite values. These checks establish that the dataset is appropriately structured for estimating average matched differences in organizational lethality.

## 6.10 Estimation of the Matched Fatality Difference

```{r}
# Recreate the matched effect on the raw fatality scale

matched_test <- t.test(
  matched_pairs$fatality_difference,
  mu = 0,
  conf.level = 0.95
)

# Calculate statistics

n_pairs <- nrow(matched_pairs)

raw_estimate <- mean(
  matched_pairs$fatality_difference
)

raw_std_error <- sd(
  matched_pairs$fatality_difference
) / sqrt(n_pairs)

# Create results table

matched_effect <- tibble(
  outcome = "Recorded fatalities",

  matched_pairs = n_pairs,

  estimate = raw_estimate,

  std_error = raw_std_error,

  ci_lower = matched_test$conf.int[1],

  ci_upper = matched_test$conf.int[2],

  p_value = matched_test$p.value
)

# Display results

print(matched_effect)

# Export results

write.csv(
  matched_effect,
  "outputs/tables/matched_effect.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The average matched difference in recorded fatalities was estimated using the 30 treatment-control pairs constructed through propensity score matching. Sponsored organizations recorded an average of 25.7 more fatalities than their matched nonsponsored controls, although this difference was not statistically significant (SE = 26.3, p = 0.337). The 95% confidence interval ranged from −28.1 to 79.4 fatalities, indicating substantial uncertainty surrounding the estimated difference. These findings are consistent with the fully adjusted regression results, which also failed to identify a statistically significant association between state sponsorship and organizational lethality. However, residual covariate imbalance, the limited matched sample, and potential unobserved confounding restrict causal interpretation.

## 6.11 Matched-Pair Analysis of Log-Transformed Fatalities

```{r}
# Additional matched analysis on the log scale

matched_log_test <- t.test(

# Calculate statistics outside tibble
```

An additional matched-pair analysis was conducted using log-transformed fatalities to reduce the influence of extreme fatality counts and facilitate comparison with the OLS regression results. The estimated average difference between sponsored organizations and their matched controls was positive (0.886), with a standard error of 0.472 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from −0.079 to 1.85. Although the estimate approached statistical significance at the 10% level (p = 0.071), it was not significant at the conventional 5% threshold. Compared with the matched analysis using raw fatalities, the log-transformed results provided somewhat stronger statistical evidence of a positive association. Nevertheless, the estimates remain sensitive to outcome measurement and are subject to limitations arising from residual covariate imbalance and potential unobserved confounding.

## 6.12 Regression Adjustment Within the Matched Sample

```{r}
# Regression adjustment within the matched sample

matched_regression <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno,
  data = matched_data,
  weights = weights
)

# Conventional regression results

summary(matched_regression)

# Cluster-robust covariance matrix by matched pair

matched_cluster_vcov <- sandwich::vcovCL(
  matched_regression,
  cluster = matched_data$subclass,
  type = "HC1"
)

# Cluster-robust inference with 30 matched pairs

matched_regression_robust <- lmtest::coeftest(
  matched_regression,
  vcov. = matched_cluster_vcov,
  df = dplyr::n_distinct(matched_data$subclass) - 1
)

print(matched_regression_robust)

# Save fitted model

saveRDS(
  matched_regression,
  "outputs/models/matched_regression.rds"
)

```

A regression-adjusted analysis was conducted within the matched sample of 60 organizations to examine the relationship between state sponsorship and log-transformed fatalities while controlling for organizational age and ideological characteristics. Standard errors were clustered by matched pair to account for dependence between matched observations. The sponsorship coefficient remained positive (0.9321) but was not statistically significant at the 5% level (cluster-robust SE = 0.4994, p = 0.072). Organizational age, religious ideology, and ethnonationalist ideology were also not statistically significant. The model explained approximately 6.5% of the variation in log-transformed fatalities. Although the positive sponsorship coefficient was consistent with the earlier matched-pair analysis, the results provide only suggestive evidence of an association and remain subject to limitations from the small matched sample, residual covariate imbalance, and potential unobserved confounding.

## 6.13 Sensitivity Analysis: Matching on Organizational Capacity

```{r}
# Secondary matching specification
# Includes potentially post-treatment characteristics

capacity_data <- regression_data %>%
  mutate(match_id = row_number())

set.seed(4422)

capacity_match <- matchit(
  sponsored ~
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno +
    factor(ordsize) +
    terrStrong +
    degree,

  data = capacity_data,

  method = "nearest",
  distance = "glm",

  estimand = "ATT",

  ratio = 1,
  replace = FALSE,

  caliper = 0.2,
  std.caliper = TRUE
)

summary(capacity_match, standardize = TRUE)

capacity_matched <- match.data(
  capacity_match,
  data = capacity_data
)

capacity_matched %>%
  count(sponsored)

saveRDS(
  capacity_match,
  "outputs/models/capacity_match_model.rds"
)
```

A secondary propensity score matching specification was estimated to assess the sensitivity of the results to the inclusion of organizational capacity characteristics. In addition to organizational age and ideological indicators, this specification incorporated organizational size, territorial strength, and network degree. The procedure matched 26 sponsored organizations with 26 nonsponsored controls, retaining 81.25% of the original sponsored sample. Matching substantially improved balance in organizational age, territorial strength, network degree, and estimated propensity scores. However, some imbalance remained in ideological characteristics and the lowest organizational size category. Compared with the primary matching specification, the capacity-adjusted procedure retained fewer sponsored organizations, illustrating a trade-off between incorporating additional matching characteristics and maintaining sample coverage. Because organizational capacity may itself be influenced by state sponsorship, this specification is interpreted as a sensitivity analysis rather than a definitive causal estimate.

## 6.14 Estimation of the Capacity-Adjusted Matched Fatality Difference

```{r}
# Confirm matched pairs are complete

capacity_structure <- capacity_matched %>%
  group_by(subclass) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    treated = sum(sponsored == 1),
    controls = sum(sponsored == 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(capacity_structure) >= 2,
  all(capacity_structure$n == 2),
  all(capacity_structure$treated == 1),
  all(capacity_structure$controls == 1)
)

capacity_pairs <- capacity_matched %>%
  group_by(subclass) %>%
  summarise(
    treated_fatalities =
      fatalities[sponsored == 1],

    control_fatalities =
      fatalities[sponsored == 0],

    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    difference =
      treated_fatalities -
      control_fatalities
  )

capacity_test <- t.test(
  capacity_pairs$difference
)

capacity_effect <- tibble(
  specification = "Capacity-adjusted matching",

  matched_pairs = nrow(capacity_pairs),

  estimate = mean(
    capacity_pairs$difference
  ),

  ci_lower = capacity_test$conf.int[1],

  ci_upper = capacity_test$conf.int[2],

  p_value = capacity_test$p.value
)

print(capacity_effect)

write.csv(
  capacity_effect,
  "outputs/tables/capacity_matching_effect.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A secondary matched-pair analysis was conducted using organizational capacity variables in addition to age and ideological characteristics. The procedure produced 26 matched pairs, and the estimated average fatality difference was approximately −122, indicating fewer recorded fatalities among sponsored organizations than their matched nonsponsored controls. However, this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.385), with a wide 95% confidence interval ranging from approximately −407 to 162 fatalities. In contrast to the positive estimate obtained from the primary matching specification, the capacity-adjusted estimate was negative, demonstrating sensitivity to the selection of matching covariates and the resulting matched sample. Because organizational capacity may be influenced by sponsorship and the alternative specification excludes additional treated organizations, these findings should be interpreted as a sensitivity analysis rather than evidence of a negative causal effect.

# 7. Robustness Analysis Using Count Models

## 7.1 Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood Regression

```{r}
# PPML with robust standard errors

poisson_model <- glm(
  fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno,

  data = regression_data,

  family = poisson(
    link = "log"
  )
)

summary(poisson_model)

# Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors

poisson_robust <- coeftest(
  poisson_model,

  vcov. = vcovHC(
    poisson_model,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)

print(poisson_robust)

# Exponentiated sponsorship coefficient
# Interpreted as a conditional mean ratio

poisson_ratio <- exp(
  coef(poisson_model)["sponsored"]
)

print(poisson_ratio)

saveRDS(
  poisson_model,
  "outputs/models/poisson_model.rds"
)
```

A Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood regression was estimated as a robustness check using recorded fatalities on their original count scale. The specification controlled for organizational age, religious ideology, and ethnonationalist ideology, with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors used for statistical inference. The estimated sponsorship coefficient was positive (0.2192), corresponding to a conditional mean ratio of 1.245, but was not statistically significant (robust SE = 0.6060, p = 0.718). Religious ideology remained positively and significantly associated with fatalities, while organizational age and ethnonationalist ideology were not significant at the 5% level. The substantial difference between conventional and robust standard errors highlights the importance of accounting for variance misspecification in the count outcome. Overall, the PPML results provide no statistically significant evidence of a sponsorship association under this specification, reinforcing the sensitivity of the findings to model choice and outcome measurement.

## 7.2 PPML Coefficient Estimates and Robust Confidence Intervals

```{r}
poisson_vcov <- vcovHC(
  poisson_model,
  type = "HC3"
)

poisson_estimates <- coef(poisson_model)

poisson_se <- sqrt(
  diag(poisson_vcov)
)

poisson_results <- tibble(
  term = names(poisson_estimates),

  estimate = as.numeric(
    poisson_estimates
  ),

  std_error = as.numeric(
    poisson_se[names(poisson_estimates)]
  ),

  ci_lower = estimate -
    1.96 * std_error,

  ci_upper = estimate +
    1.96 * std_error,

  mean_ratio = exp(estimate),

  ratio_lower = exp(ci_lower),

  ratio_upper = exp(ci_upper)
)

print(poisson_results, n = Inf)

write.csv(
  poisson_results,
  "outputs/tables/poisson_results.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust confidence intervals were calculated for the PPML regression coefficients, and the estimates were exponentiated to express their associations with expected fatality counts as conditional mean ratios. State sponsorship had an estimated mean ratio of 1.245, corresponding to approximately 24.5% higher expected fatalities among sponsored organizations after adjusting for organizational age and ideology. However, the 95% confidence interval ranged from 0.380 to 4.08, indicating that the association was not statistically significant. Religious ideology exhibited a positive and statistically significant association with fatalities, with an estimated mean ratio of 8.95, although its confidence interval was relatively wide. Organizational age and ethnonationalist ideology were not statistically significant at the 5% level. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial uncertainty surrounding the sponsorship estimate and reinforce the importance of robust statistical inference when analyzing highly dispersed fatality counts.

## 7.3 Outlier Identification and Regression Influence Diagnostics

```{r}
# Identify organizations with the highest recorded fatalities

highest_fatalities <- analysis_data %>%
  arrange(desc(fatalities)) %>%
  select(
    mastertccode3606,
    group,
    sponsored,
    fatalities,
    OrgAge,
    ordsize,
    terrStrong,
    degree
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Display highest-fatality organizations

print(
  highest_fatalities,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

# Export highest-fatality table

write.csv(
  highest_fatalities,
  "outputs/tables/highest_fatalities.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Calculate influence diagnostics for the fully adjusted OLS model

regression_influence <- regression_data %>%
  mutate(
    cooks_distance = cooks.distance(model4)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cooks_distance))

# Calculate conventional Cook's distance screening threshold

cooks_threshold <- 4 / nobs(model4)

# Identify influential observations

influential_observations <- regression_influence %>%
  mutate(
    above_threshold = cooks_distance > cooks_threshold
  ) %>%
  select(
    group,
    sponsored,
    fatalities,
    cooks_distance,
    above_threshold
  ) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Display influence diagnostics

print(
  influential_observations,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

# Summarize influence screening

influence_summary <- tibble(
  observations = nobs(model4),

  cooks_threshold = cooks_threshold,

  observations_above_threshold = sum(
    regression_influence$cooks_distance > cooks_threshold
  ),

  maximum_cooks_distance = max(
    regression_influence$cooks_distance
  )
)

print(influence_summary, width = Inf)

# Export influence diagnostics

write.csv(
  regression_influence,
  "outputs/tables/regression_influence.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.csv(
  influence_summary,
  "outputs/tables/influence_summary.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

Potential outliers and influential observations were examined to assess the sensitivity of the regression analysis to extreme organizational characteristics and fatality counts. The dataset contained substantial variation in lethality, including organizations with exceptionally high recorded fatalities. Cook's distance was calculated for the fully adjusted OLS model to identify observations exerting disproportionate influence on the estimated regression coefficients. The results indicated that influential observations were not necessarily those with the highest fatality counts, suggesting that unusual combinations of organizational characteristics may also affect model estimates. These diagnostics provide a basis for subsequent sensitivity testing, although observations should not be excluded solely because they exhibit elevated Cook's distance values.

## 7.4 Sensitivity Analysis Excluding Extreme Fatality Counts

```{r}
# Sensitivity to extremely high fatality counts

fatality_cutoff <- quantile(
  regression_data$fatalities,
  probs = 0.99,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

trimmed_data <- regression_data %>%
  filter(fatalities <= fatality_cutoff)

trimmed_model <- lm(
  log_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno +
    factor(ordsize) +
    terrStrong +
    degree,

  data = trimmed_data
)

coeftest(
  trimmed_model,

  vcov. = vcovHC(
    trimmed_model,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)

trimmed_results <- robust_results(
  trimmed_model,
  "Top 1% excluded"
)

write.csv(
  trimmed_results,
  "outputs/tables/outlier_sensitivity.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess whether organizations with exceptionally high fatality counts influenced the fully adjusted OLS results. Observations exceeding the 99th percentile of recorded fatalities were excluded, and the regression was re-estimated using the original set of organizational controls. The sponsorship coefficient increased from 0.0890 in the full sample to 0.2087 in the trimmed sample but remained statistically insignificant using HC3 robust standard errors (SE = 0.3759, p = 0.579). Religious ideology, organizational size, territorial strength, and network degree retained positive and statistically significant associations with log-transformed fatalities. These findings suggest that the lack of a statistically significant sponsorship association in the fully adjusted model is not solely attributable to organizations with extreme fatality counts. Nevertheless, the results remain observational and do not eliminate concerns regarding unmeasured confounding or other influential observations.

## 7.5 Logistic Regression of Fatality Incidence

```{r}
# Binary-outcome sensitivity analysis

incidence_model <- glm(
  positive_fatalities ~
    sponsored +
    OrgAge +
    containrelig +
    containethno,

  data = regression_data,

  family = binomial(
    link = "logit"
  )
)

summary(incidence_model)

coeftest(
  incidence_model,

  vcov. = vcovHC(
    incidence_model,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)

# Average model-predicted probability by
# setting sponsorship to each condition

predict_0 <- regression_data %>%
  mutate(sponsored = 0)

predict_1 <- regression_data %>%
  mutate(sponsored = 1)

probability_comparison <- tibble(
  sponsorship = c(
    "Not sponsored",
    "Sponsored"
  ),

  average_predicted_probability = c(
    mean(
      predict(
        incidence_model,
        newdata = predict_0,
        type = "response"
      )
    ),

    mean(
      predict(
        incidence_model,
        newdata = predict_1,
        type = "response"
      )
    )
  )
)

print(probability_comparison)

write.csv(
  probability_comparison,
  "outputs/tables/incidence_model_probabilities.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

A logistic regression was estimated as an additional robustness check to examine whether state sponsorship was associated with the likelihood of an organization recording at least one fatality. The model controlled for organizational age, religious ideology, and ethnonationalist ideology, with HC3 robust standard errors used for inference. The sponsorship coefficient was positive (0.6265) but not statistically significant (SE = 0.5922, p = 0.290). Organizational age and both ideological indicators exhibited positive and statistically significant associations with fatality incidence. The average model-predicted probability of recording fatalities was 38.3% under the nonsponsored condition and 50.3% under the sponsored condition, representing an estimated difference of approximately 12 percentage points. However, the lack of statistical significance for the sponsorship coefficient indicates insufficient evidence of an adjusted association in this specification. These results further demonstrate that the estimated relationship between state sponsorship and organizational lethality depends on the outcome measure and model specification.

## 7.6 Comparison of Primary and Capacity-Adjusted Matching Estimates

```{r}
# Compare matching results on the raw fatality scale

matching_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  matched_effect %>%
    transmute(
      specification = "Age and ideology matching",
      matched_pairs,
      estimate,
      ci_lower,
      ci_upper,
      p_value
    ),

  capacity_effect %>%
    select(
      specification,
      matched_pairs,
      estimate,
      ci_lower,
      ci_upper,
      p_value
    )
)

# Display comparison as a regular tibble

print(
  matching_comparison,
  n = Inf,
  width = Inf
)

# Export matching comparison

write.csv(
  matching_comparison,
  "outputs/tables/matching_comparison.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

```

The primary and capacity-adjusted matching estimates were compared to evaluate the sensitivity of the estimated sponsorship association to the selection of matching variables. The primary specification, matching on organizational age and ideology, produced an average difference of 25.67 additional fatalities among sponsored organizations, although the estimate was not statistically significant (p = 0.337). In contrast, the capacity-adjusted specification produced a negative average difference of 122.23 fatalities, which was also statistically insignificant (p = 0.385). Both confidence intervals included zero, indicating substantial uncertainty regarding the direction and magnitude of the association. The reversal in the estimated coefficient demonstrates sensitivity to matching specification and sample composition. Because organizational capacity may be influenced by state sponsorship, the secondary specification is interpreted as a robustness check rather than a definitive causal estimate.

## 7.7 Visualization of Matching Sensitivity Estimates

```{r}
figure8 <- ggplot(
  matching_comparison,
  aes(
    x = estimate,
    y = specification
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,

  ) +
  geom_errorbarh(
    aes(
      xmin = ci_lower,
      xmax = ci_upper
    ),

  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Matched Sponsorship Associations",
    subtitle = "Estimated differences in recorded fatalities",
    x = "Matched mean fatality difference",
    y = "Matching specification",
    caption = "Intervals are preliminary pair-based 95% CIs"
  ) +

print(figure8)

ggsave(
  "outputs/figures/figure8_matching_estimates.pdf",
```

Figure 8 compares the estimated differences in recorded fatalities between sponsored organizations and matched nonsponsored controls under the two propensity score matching specifications. The primary specification produced a positive average difference of 25.67 fatalities, while the capacity-adjusted specification produced a negative difference of 122.23 fatalities. However, the 95% confidence intervals for both estimates included zero, indicating that neither association was statistically significant at the 5% level. The substantial difference between the point estimates highlights the sensitivity of the matching results to covariate selection and changes in matched sample composition. Because organizational capacity may be influenced by sponsorship, and residual confounding remains possible, these results should be interpreted as evidence of methodological sensitivity rather than definitive causal effects.

This figure summarizes how the estimated sponsorship coefficient changes across the four OLS specifications using log-transformed fatalities as the outcome. Overall, the figure shows that the estimated sponsorship association is sensitive to model specification, especially to the inclusion of organizational capacity and network-related controls.

The final analytical dataset, regression models, matching samples, and supporting outputs were preserved to support reproducibility and verification of the econometric analysis. The study included 395 terrorist organizations, of which 32 were classified as state-sponsored. Descriptive results indicated that sponsored organizations recorded fatalities more frequently and exhibited higher average lethality than nonsponsored organizations. However, the initially significant sponsorship association weakened substantially after adjustment for organizational characteristics. Propensity score matching, Poisson regression, and logistic regression analyses generally produced statistically insignificant sponsorship estimates, while alternative matching specifications demonstrated sensitivity to covariate selection and sample composition. Overall, the findings suggest that observable organizational characteristics play an important role in explaining differences in terrorist organization lethality, although limitations related to observational data, residual imbalance, potential post-treatment controls, and unobserved confounding prevent definitive causal conclusions.
